holding_summary: A traveler who lodged at a hotel and deposited a trunk there sued the innkeepers for money stolen from the trunk; the court held inn-keepers are liable as depositaries for guests' effects unless the loss occurred through forcible exterior breaking-in or other extraordinary violence, and that this default liability could only be limited by posting the statutory notice under the 1860 Act.

quotes.text: Inn-keepers are responsible, as .depositaries, for effects brought to their house by travelers who lodge therein; they are responsible even when their effects are stolen, unless they show that the same were stolen by force and arms, or with exterior breaking of doors (ou avec effraction extérieure), or by any other extraordinary violence (ou autre force majeure).

Inn-keepers are responsible, as .depositaries, for effects brought to their house by travelers who lodge therein; they are responsible even when their effects are stolen, unless they show that the same were stolen by force and arms, or with exterior breaking of doors (ou avec effraction extérieure), or by any other extraordinary violence (ou autre force majeure).

notes: Not a case about the legality of letting rooms/dwelling per se; it treats operation of a hotel as an established lawful business and applies ordinary depositary/bailment liability rules to the innkeeper-guest relationship. Marked favorable at low weight because it recognizes and enforces the lodging relationship rather than restricting it.
Long-term (50-year) ground lease vs. emphyteusis characterization for tax-liability purposes between an orphan asylum and a lessee. Not a dwelling/room letting or lodging dispute.

Marital separation from 'bed and board' and community-property division; surety liability on an injunction bond. 'Bed and board' here is the marital-separation term of art, unrelated to lodging-for-pay.

Furniture-ownership dispute (dation en payement) between two women; opinion notes in passing that plaintiff 'rented a room from the defendant and boarded with her a short time,' but the court decides nothing about the legal character of that boarding arrangement — the holding turns entirely on title to furniture and evidentiary admissibility. Passing-mention case per instructions.
